turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: They sent me here from the station. I was moving the airway bags around in the bay, putting them in this pattern that felt… right. I kept saying the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, and when my lieutenant told me to stop, I couldn’t step away. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad somehow.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes repetitive, contextually inappropriate arranging and verbal repetition, with inability to disengage when instructed.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports repetitive arranging and saying numbers aloud in a fixed sequence to prevent a feared negative outcome.

turns.doctor_question: When you were arranging the bags and repeating the numbers, did part of you recognize that this was excessive or didn't make sense, and did you feel upset or anxious trying to resist doing it?
turns.patient_response: I mean… yeah, I knew it probably looked excessive. I knew my lieutenant wanted me to stop, and I couldn’t really explain it in a normal way. But at the time it felt like the pattern was right, and if I stepped away or stopped saying the dispatch numbers, the whole bay would go bad somehow. So I just kept doing it.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes persistently arranging bags into a pattern and repeating dispatch numbers despite being told to stop and being unable to step away.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The repetitive arranging and number repetition were continued because the patient believed that stopping the sequence would cause something bad to happen.

turns.doctor_question: Has this kind of thing—needing to arrange things in a very particular way or repeat certain actions because something bad might happen otherwise—been happening to you on and off for a while now, or is this the first time you've experienced something like this?
turns.patient_response: This is what they sent me here for. At the station I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern that felt right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant told me to stop, but I couldn’t step away because it felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes repetitive arranging of airway bags and repeating dispatch numbers, with inability to stop because breaking the sequence felt threatening.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from this recent incident, have you always been the kind of person who needs things extremely orderly, exact, or done 'just right' in most areas of your life—like at home, with schedules, or in relationships—or is this pattern of needing to arrange things and repeat numbers something new and different from how you've always been?
turns.patient_response: This is more new for me. I mean, I’ve always liked things organized enough, but not like this. The stuff with the camera and the paperwork, and then what happened at the station with the bags and numbers… that’s been going on maybe the last two months. That’s when people started getting alarmed.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned some trouble with a camera and paperwork around the same time—can you tell me more about what was happening with those?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah. I started thinking the injury review people, and some of the supervisors, were watching me through the station cameras. Not just normal security—watching me specifically.

And the paperwork… my triage notes would come back different, or it felt like they were being changed to make it look like I was unsafe on calls. They kept saying it was just routine review or normal paperwork stuff, but I don’t buy that. It felt like they were building something against me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed-seeming belief that injury review staff and supervisors were specifically surveilling him through cameras and altering records to build a case against him despite routine-review explanations.

turns.patient_response: I don’t think so. I mean, I haven’t been seeing things like that. And voices… no, not really. I hear normal station noise and people talking when they’re there, but I haven’t noticed voices that nobody else hears.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies seeing things and denies hearing voices that nobody else hears, while attributing heard sounds to normal station noise and people talking.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned this has been going on for about two months—have these beliefs about being watched and your paperwork being altered been continuously present during that whole time, or have they come and gone?
turns.patient_response: It’s been pretty constant. Some days it’s more on my mind than others, but I haven’t really stopped believing it. I know they’re watching me through the station cameras, and I know the triage notes are being changed to make me look unsafe, even when they keep saying it’s just routine review or paperwork.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, new medications, or used any alcohol or drugs (including supplements) around the time these beliefs and behaviors started?
turns.patient_response: I’m not really sure. I don’t remember any illness or head injury around when it started. Medications… I’d have to think about it, but nothing stands out to me. And I wasn’t doing anything different with alcohol or drugs that I can point to.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of these specific incidents with the cameras, paperwork, and the bags, how have you been managing with your daily routine—things like your work performance overall, taking care of yourself, and your relationships with family or friends?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, not well. I can’t really work on the ambulance anymore, and even when they put me on desk stuff, my notes and the equipment checks got… unreliable, I guess. They ended up taking me off the schedule.

At home I’ve fallen behind on things, and I’ve mostly stopped seeing friends. I’m not keeping up the way I used to.

symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports having mostly stopped seeing friends, indicating social withdrawal.
